name: Collider physics
question: What are the fundamental particles and forces, and how do they behave at the highest energies we can create in a laboratory?
overview: Collider physics studies particle collisions at the highest centre-of-mass energies achievable in the laboratory: today 13.6 TeV proton–proton collisions at the LHC, building on electron–positron data from LEP and SLC and the proton–antiproton Tevatron programme. It covers precision Standard Model measurements (Higgs, electroweak, top quark, QCD) and direct searches for new particles and interactions. Reconstructed final states of jets, leptons, photons and missing transverse momentum are compared with theory predictions at next-to-next-to-leading order. Facilities under study include the HL-LHC, electron–positron Higgs factories (FCC-ee, CEPC, ILC, C^3, CLIC), a ~100 TeV hadron collider (FCC-hh) and a multi-TeV muon collider.

name: Flavor physics
question: Why are there three copies of each type of matter particle, and why do they transform into one another in the specific pattern we observe?
overview: Flavor physics studies transitions between the three generations of quarks and leptons. In the Standard Model, quark flavor change is governed by the CKM matrix and flavor-changing neutral currents arise only at loop level, so rare decays, meson mixing and CP asymmetries in K, D and B hadrons are sensitive to new particles at mass scales of 10^3 to 10^5 TeV, far beyond direct collider reach. CP violation is also a necessary ingredient for the observed matter–antimatter asymmetry of the universe, although the Standard Model amount is too small. Major facilities are Belle II at SuperKEKB, LHCb and the general-purpose LHC detectors, BESIII, NA62 and KOTO.

name: Neutrino physics
question: What are neutrinos, the most abundant matter particles, really like: how heavy are they, how do they mix, and are they their own antiparticles?
overview: Neutrino physics addresses the least understood Standard Model fermions: their masses and ordering, mixing and CP violation, Dirac or Majorana nature, interactions with nuclei, possible sterile partners, and their role as astrophysical messengers. Neutrino sources span nuclear reactors, accelerator beams, the Sun, cosmic-ray air showers, supernovae, the Earth's interior and distant cosmic accelerators, with energies from meV (relic neutrinos) to beyond 10 PeV. Detection uses charged-current and neutral-current scattering in large water, ice, scintillator or liquid-argon detectors, and precision spectroscopy of beta decays. Non-zero neutrino masses, established by oscillation experiments, are the only laboratory evidence for physics beyond the minimal Standard Model.
observables: flux and spectrum from each source

name: Dark matter
question: What is the invisible matter that makes up about 85% of all matter in the universe, and can we detect it as a particle?
overview: Gravitational evidence from galaxy rotation curves, gravitational lensing, the cosmic microwave background and large-scale structure implies that about 27% of the energy density of the universe, roughly 85% of its matter, is non-luminous dark matter with no Standard Model candidate. Particle searches follow three complementary strategies: direct detection of Galactic dark matter scattering in low-background detectors, indirect detection of annihilation or decay products, and production at accelerators. Candidates range from ultralight wave-like fields such as the QCD axion (down to 10^-22 eV) through sub-GeV hidden-sector particles to weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs) and primordial black holes. No non-gravitational detection has been confirmed.

name: Precision and rare processes
question: Can extremely precise measurements, or searches for processes that should almost never happen, reveal new particles too heavy or too weakly coupled to produce directly?
overview: Precision measurements and searches for forbidden or extremely rare processes test the Standard Model indirectly. Quantum corrections from heavy or feebly interacting new particles shift observables such as the muon anomalous magnetic moment, electric dipole moments and rare-decay rates, so a measurement at the part-per-million or 10^-13 branching-fraction level can probe mass scales of hundreds of TeV. The area also includes searches for new light or long-lived states with tiny couplings at intense beams and beam dumps: heavy neutral leptons, dark photons and other long-lived particles. Experiments are typically small or medium scale, at PSI, Fermilab, J-PARC, CERN's SPS and LHC forward regions, and electron–positron colliders.

name: Astroparticle physics
question: What can particles arriving from space, from cosmic rays to gamma rays and neutrinos, tell us about the most extreme objects in the universe and about fundamental physics?
overview: Astroparticle physics uses the universe as a laboratory, detecting cosmic rays, gamma rays, neutrinos and, increasingly, gravitational waves to study cosmic accelerators and to test fundamental physics at energies and distances unreachable on Earth. Ground-based instruments include extensive air-shower arrays, imaging atmospheric Cherenkov telescopes, and cubic-kilometre neutrino telescopes in ice and water; space-borne instruments measure charged cosmic rays and gamma rays directly above the atmosphere. Central questions are the origin of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays, the identification of PeV-scale Galactic accelerators, the sources of high-energy neutrinos, and indirect signatures of dark matter, Lorentz-invariance violation and axion–photon conversion.

name: Nuclear and heavy-ion physics
question: How does the strong force behave in dense, hot nuclear matter and inside nuclei, and what does that tell particle physics?
overview: This area covers the interface between nuclear and particle physics where the questions are materially particle-physics questions: quantum chromodynamics under extreme temperature and density in relativistic heavy-ion collisions at RHIC and the LHC, the phase diagram of QCD matter, and hadron and nucleon structure studied at Jefferson Lab and the planned Electron–Ion Collider. Low-energy nuclear physics, nuclear structure and applied nuclear science are outside the atlas scope unless a facility participates directly in a high-energy-physics question, for example through neutrinoless double beta decay or coherent neutrino scattering. Heavy-ion programmes at ALICE, ATLAS, CMS, LHCb, STAR, sPHENIX and PHENIX are included.

name: Instrumentation and detector technology
question: What new detector and accelerator technologies make the next generation of particle-physics experiments possible?
overview: Instrumentation covers the sensors, electronics, data acquisition, software and accelerator technology that determine what experiments can measure. Progress in this area, from wire chambers and silicon pixel detectors to liquid-argon time projection chambers and superconducting magnets, has repeatedly enabled discoveries, and technology milestones (first operation of a new detector type at scale, record timing or energy resolution) are tracked in the atlas as results of type technology_milestone. Community roadmaps, notably the 2021 ECFA Detector R&D Roadmap and the Snowmass 2021 Instrumentation Frontier report, organise the effort into themes such as solid-state tracking, calorimetry, photon detection, gaseous and noble-liquid detectors, quantum sensing, and trigger and readout systems.

name: Higgs physics
question: What is the Higgs boson, does it behave exactly as the Standard Model predicts, and does it give mass to every other particle in the way theory says?
overview: The Higgs boson, discovered by ATLAS and CMS in 2012 with a mass near 125 GeV, is the quantum of the field responsible for electroweak symmetry breaking. Its couplings to the W and Z bosons and to third-generation fermions (top, bottom, tau) have been measured at the LHC and agree with Standard Model predictions within current uncertainties of roughly 5–20% depending on the channel. Open questions include the Higgs self-coupling, which fixes the shape of the Higgs potential and is accessible through di-Higgs production; couplings to second-generation fermions, where H→μμ has been seen with about 3σ evidence but not yet observed; CP properties; the total width; and possible invisible or exotic decays. The HL-LHC and proposed Higgs factories target per-cent-level coupling precision.
observables: signal strengths μ per production and decay mode
CP quantum numbers of HVV and Hff couplings
di-Higgs cross section and trilinear self-coupling λ_HHH
simplified template and differential cross sections

name: Electroweak physics
question: How precisely do the W and Z bosons behave, and do precision measurements of the weak force reveal cracks in the Standard Model?
overview: Electroweak physics tests the SU(2)×U(1) gauge structure of the Standard Model through precision measurements of W and Z boson properties and multi-boson production. LEP and SLC fixed the Z lineshape parameters, asymmetries and the number of light neutrino species; the Tevatron and LHC measure the W mass, the effective weak mixing angle, and diboson and triboson cross sections. Because m_W, m_Z, m_t, m_H and α_s are related by loop corrections, a global electroweak fit tests internal consistency. The 2022 CDF W-mass measurement is in tension with the fit and with ATLAS, LHCb and CMS measurements, which agree with the Standard Model. Vector-boson scattering and anomalous gauge couplings, usually interpreted in the SMEFT framework, probe new physics at scales beyond direct reach.
observables: W boson mass m_W and width Γ_W
Z mass, width and lineshape parameters
diboson and triboson cross sections (WW, WZ, ZZ, Wγ, Zγ)
anomalous triple and quartic gauge coupling limits
W helicity fractions and charge asymmetry

name: Top-quark physics
question: Why is the top quark so heavy, and does the heaviest known particle behave exactly as the Standard Model predicts in how it is produced and decays?
overview: The top quark, discovered at the Tevatron in 1995 by CDF and DØ, is the heaviest known elementary particle (about 172.5 GeV) and decays via t→Wb before hadronising, so its spin information is passed to its decay products. At the LHC it is produced copiously in pairs through the strong interaction and singly through electroweak processes. Measurements cover the mass, now with sub-GeV precision but with subtleties in relating the directly measured mass to the pole or MS-bar mass; total and differential cross sections; the Wtb vertex structure; spin correlations and quantum entanglement; charge asymmetries; and associated production with W, Z, γ and Higgs bosons, including four-top production. The large top Yukawa coupling makes the top quark central to vacuum stability and to many Standard Model extensions.
observables: tt̄ cross section, total and differential
W helicity fractions in top decay
tt̄H, tt̄Z, tt̄W and tt̄tt̄ cross sections

name: Quantum chromodynamics
question: How does the strong force bind quarks and gluons, how strong is it at different energies, and how are protons and other hadrons built from their constituents?
overview: Quantum chromodynamics (QCD) is the SU(3) gauge theory of quarks and gluons. Its coupling α_s decreases with energy (asymptotic freedom), so hard-scattering processes are computed perturbatively, while confinement and hadron structure require lattice QCD or non-perturbative modelling. Collider and e+e− experiments measure jet cross sections, event shapes and multi-jet ratios to extract α_s(m_Z) ≈ 0.118, and combine deep-inelastic scattering (HERA), Drell–Yan and jet data to determine parton distribution functions. Other active areas are hadron spectroscopy, including exotic multiquark candidates such as the X(3872) and the pentaquark states reported by LHCb; fragmentation and hadronisation; diffraction and small-x physics; and the transverse-momentum-dependent and spin structure of the nucleon, a focus of Jefferson Lab and the future Electron–Ion Collider.
observables: strong coupling α_s(m_Z) and its running
inclusive jet, dijet and multijet cross sections
hadron masses, widths and quantum numbers
exotic hadron spectrum (tetraquark and pentaquark candidates)

name: Direct searches for new particles at colliders
question: Are there undiscovered heavy particles, such as supersymmetric partners or new force carriers, that colliders could produce directly?
overview: Direct searches look for new particles produced in collisions and identified by their decay products: resonances in dijet, dilepton, diphoton or top-pair mass spectra; final states with large missing transverse momentum from invisible particles as predicted by supersymmetry or dark-matter models; leptoquarks; vector-like quarks; heavy gauge bosons (W′, Z′); extra Higgs bosons; and microscopic black holes or extra dimensions. No new particle has been observed at the LHC beyond the Higgs boson; typical exclusions reach several TeV for strongly produced states and about 1 TeV for electroweak-scale supersymmetric partners, with gaps in compressed and long-lived scenarios. Results are reported as cross-section limits and interpreted in simplified models, complete models, or effective field theories, which is why the same search constrains many theories.
observables: 95% CL cross-section upper limits versus mass
mass exclusions in simplified models (gluino, squark, stop, chargino, neutralino)
resonance mass spectra (dijet, dilepton, diphoton, tt̄)

name: Flavor mixing and CP violation
question: Why does matter behave slightly differently from antimatter, and do quark transitions follow the single pattern that the Standard Model predicts?
overview: In the Standard Model, quark flavor transitions and all CP violation in the quark sector are governed by the Cabibbo–Kobayashi–Maskawa (CKM) matrix, a 3×3 unitary matrix with one irreducible phase. Experiments test whether measurements of its magnitudes (from semileptonic and leptonic decays and meson mixing) and angles (from CP asymmetries in B, D and K decays) are consistent with a single unitarity triangle. CP violation has been established in the K (1964), B (2001, BaBar and Belle) and D (2019, LHCb) meson systems, in both mixing-induced and direct forms. Because flavor-changing neutral currents arise only at loop level in the Standard Model, rare and loop-induced processes are sensitive to new physics at mass scales far above direct collider reach. Global fits currently show consistency with the CKM picture.
observables: indirect CP violation ε_K and direct ε′/ε
time-dependent CP asymmetries S_f and C_f

name: B physics
question: What can the decays of particles containing bottom quarks tell us about new forces or particles that are too heavy to produce directly?
overview: B physics studies hadrons containing b quarks, produced at e+e− B factories (BaBar, Belle, Belle II at the Υ(4S)) and at hadron colliders (LHCb, CMS, ATLAS, and formerly CDF and DØ). Measurements include lifetimes, the mixing frequencies Δm_d and Δm_s, CP asymmetries, and semileptonic decays used to extract |V_cb| and |V_ub|, where inclusive and exclusive determinations have long differed at the 2–3σ level. Rare decays probe loop-level physics: B_s→μ+μ− agrees with the Standard Model; b→sℓℓ angular observables and branching fractions lie below predictions while the lepton-universality ratios R_K and R_K* returned to Standard Model agreement in 2022. The ratios R(D) and R(D*), testing τ/ℓ universality, exceed predictions by about 3σ combined. Belle II and the upgraded LHCb aim to sharpen these tests.
observables: b→sℓℓ branching fractions and angular observables (P_5′)

name: Rare kaon physics
question: Can extremely rare decays of kaons, which happen in fewer than one in ten billion cases, reveal new particles or forces?
overview: Rare kaon decays probe flavor-changing neutral currents at low energy with exceptional theoretical cleanliness. The decays K+→π+νν̄ and K_L→π0νν̄ are dominated by short-distance physics and their Standard Model branching fractions are predicted to a few per cent, around 8×10^-11 and 3×10^-11 respectively. NA62 at the CERN SPS reported the first observation of K+→π+νν̄ at above 5σ in 2024, with a branching fraction of about 13×10^-11, roughly 1.7σ above the prediction; KOTO at J-PARC sets upper limits on K_L→π0νν̄ and KOTO II is proposed. Other channels include K_L→π0ℓ+ℓ−, K_S→μ+μ−, lepton-flavor and lepton-number violating kaon decays, and precision tests of lepton universality and |V_us| in K→ℓν and K→πℓν decays.

name: Charm physics
question: Do charm quarks, the only up-type quarks whose mixing and CP violation can be measured, behave as the Standard Model predicts?
overview: Charm hadrons offer the only accessible up-type-quark system in which meson mixing and CP violation can be studied. D0–D̄0 mixing is well established with mixing parameters x and y below about one per cent; LHCb observed direct CP violation in the difference of asymmetries in D0→K+K− and D0→π+π− decays in 2019, ΔA_CP = (−15.4 ± 2.9)×10^-4, larger than naive Standard Model estimates but hard to interpret because long-distance contributions are not calculable from first principles. Charm also provides decay constants and form factors that validate lattice QCD (BESIII, CLEO-c), precise |V_cs| and |V_cd|, rare decays such as D0→μ+μ−, and a rich spectroscopy of charmed baryons and charmonium-like exotic states.
observables: ΔA_CP and A_CP in individual channels
charmed baryon lifetimes and branching fractions
charmonium-like exotic state masses and widths

name: Neutrino oscillations
question: Why do neutrinos change from one type to another as they travel, which neutrino is heaviest, and do neutrinos and antineutrinos oscillate differently?
overview: Neutrino oscillations, established by Super-Kamiokande with atmospheric neutrinos (1998) and SNO with solar neutrinos (2001–2002), show that neutrinos have mass and that flavor states are superpositions of mass states described by the PMNS matrix, with three mixing angles, one Dirac CP phase and two independent mass-squared differences. θ_12 and Δm²_21 come from solar and KamLAND data; θ_13 from reactor experiments (Daya Bay, RENO, Double Chooz); θ_23 and |Δm²_32| from atmospheric and long-baseline accelerator experiments (T2K, NOvA, Super-K, IceCube). The remaining unknowns are the mass ordering (normal or inverted), the θ_23 octant, and δ_CP, where T2K and NOvA are individually compatible with CP conservation but jointly disfavour some parameter regions. JUNO, DUNE and Hyper-Kamiokande are designed to resolve them.

name: Neutrino interactions and cross sections
question: How do neutrinos interact with atomic nuclei, and how well can we model those interactions, which every accelerator neutrino measurement depends on?
overview: Neutrino–nucleus scattering cross sections in the 0.1–20 GeV range are among the largest systematic uncertainties for accelerator-based oscillation experiments. Processes include charged-current quasi-elastic scattering, resonant and coherent pion production, deep-inelastic scattering and neutral-current channels; nuclear effects such as Fermi motion, multi-nucleon (2p2h) correlations and final-state interactions distort the observed kinematics and bias energy reconstruction. MiniBooNE, MINERvA, the T2K near detectors, NOvA, MicroBooNE and ArgoNeuT have measured cross sections on carbon, water, argon and other targets; the SBN detectors and the DUNE near detector will improve argon data. Neutrino–electron scattering and inverse beta decay are precisely calculable and serve as flux normalisation, while high-energy data from NuTeV, CCFR and FASERν test QCD and the weak mixing angle.
observables: CC inclusive, CC0π, CC1π and CCQE cross sections versus E_ν
NC π0 and NC elastic cross sections
deep-inelastic structure functions and sin²θ_W from ν-N
energy-reconstruction bias and transverse kinematic imbalance

name: Supernova neutrinos
question: What happens inside a collapsing star, and can the burst of neutrinos from the next nearby supernova reveal how stars explode and what neutrinos are like?
overview: A core-collapse supernova emits about 3×10^53 erg, some 99% of the released gravitational binding energy, as neutrinos and antineutrinos of all flavors over roughly ten seconds, with mean energies of 10–15 MeV. The only detection so far is SN 1987A: about two dozen events in Kamiokande-II, IMB and Baksan, which confirmed the basic picture and constrained neutrino mass, lifetime and exotic couplings. A Galactic supernova today would yield thousands of events in Super-Kamiokande, JUNO, IceCube, DUNE and other detectors; the time, energy and flavor structure would probe the neutronisation burst, accretion and cooling phases, collective flavor conversion and the mass ordering. The SNEWS network coordinates early alerts. Searches for the diffuse supernova neutrino background (Super-Kamiokande with gadolinium) are approaching predicted flux levels.
observables: event rate versus time (burst time profile)
ν̄_e energy spectrum via inverse beta decay
ν_e neutronisation burst via ν_e–Ar charged-current and ν–e elastic scattering
total emitted energy and mean energies per flavor

name: Solar neutrinos
question: How does the Sun produce its energy, and what did the missing solar neutrinos teach us about the neutrino itself?
overview: Solar neutrinos are produced in the proton–proton chain and the CNO cycle. The Homestake chlorine experiment (from 1968) measured a deficit relative to the standard solar model, confirmed by Kamiokande, GALLEX/GNO and SAGE; SNO's charged-current, neutral-current and elastic-scattering measurements (2001–2002) showed that the total 8B flux matched the model while the electron-flavor fraction was about one third, establishing flavor conversion through the MSW matter effect. Borexino measured the 7Be, pep, pp and, in 2020, CNO fluxes, the last confirming that the CNO cycle operates in the Sun. Current topics include the day–night asymmetry, the 8B spectrum shape at low energy, solar metallicity from CNO neutrinos, and using the Sun as a source for oscillation and non-standard-interaction tests in Super-Kamiokande, SNO+, JUNO, and large dark-matter detectors.
observables: 8B, 7Be, pep, pp, CNO and hep neutrino fluxes
electron survival probability P_ee versus energy
Δm²_21 and sin²θ_12 from solar data

name: Atmospheric neutrinos
question: How do neutrinos made by cosmic rays hitting the atmosphere behave over distances from tens to thousands of kilometres through the Earth?
overview: Cosmic rays striking the atmosphere produce pions and kaons whose decays yield muon and electron neutrinos and antineutrinos from about 100 MeV to well above 1 TeV, over baselines from about 15 km (downward) to about 13,000 km (upward through the Earth). Super-Kamiokande's 1998 observation of a zenith-angle-dependent muon-neutrino deficit was the first compelling evidence for neutrino oscillations. Atmospheric samples now constrain θ_23 and |Δm²_32|, and through Earth matter effects in the 2–8 GeV range are sensitive to the mass ordering; Super-Kamiokande and IceCube DeepCore have also observed tau-neutrino appearance. Flux modelling relies on cosmic-ray spectra and hadronic-interaction models, calibrated against muon data. Super-Kamiokande, IceCube DeepCore and the IceCube Upgrade, KM3NeT/ORCA, JUNO, Hyper-Kamiokande and DUNE continue this programme.
observables: zenith-angle distributions by flavor and energy
mass-ordering sensitivity via resonant matter effects
atmospheric flux normalisation and ν/ν̄ ratio
muon and electron neutrino flux ratio

name: Reactor neutrinos
question: What can the antineutrinos streaming out of nuclear reactors teach us about neutrino mixing and about which neutrino is the heaviest?
overview: Nuclear reactors are intense, pure sources of electron antineutrinos from beta decays of fission fragments of 235U, 239Pu, 238U and 241Pu, with energies up to about 10 MeV, detected through inverse beta decay in liquid scintillator. The Cowan–Reines experiment at Savannah River (1956) provided the first detection of neutrinos. KamLAND (2002) observed disappearance at a mean baseline of about 180 km, confirming the solar oscillation solution; Daya Bay, RENO and Double Chooz (2012) measured θ_13 at 1–2 km. JUNO, at about 53 km, aims to determine the mass ordering from the interference of the Δm²_31 and Δm²_32 oscillation patterns and to measure several parameters to sub-per-cent precision. A spectral bump near 5 MeV and a flux deficit relative to older predictions motivated revised flux models and short-baseline sterile-neutrino searches.
observables: antineutrino flux and spectrum per fission, by isotope

name: High-energy astrophysical neutrinos
question: Where do the highest-energy neutrinos in the universe come from, and what do they reveal about extreme cosmic accelerators?
overview: Astrophysical neutrinos above about 10 TeV were discovered by IceCube in 2013 as an approximately isotropic diffuse flux exceeding the atmospheric background. Sources identified since include the blazar TXS 0506+056 (2017, with a coincident gamma-ray flare, about 3σ), the Seyfert galaxy NGC 1068 (4.2σ, 2022) and the Galactic plane (4.5σ, 2023). Cubic-kilometre Cherenkov detectors in ice (IceCube) and water (ANTARES, KM3NeT, Baikal-GVD) reconstruct through-going muon tracks and cascades; KM3NeT reported an event with estimated energy of about 220 PeV in 2025. Radio detectors (ARA, ARIANNA, RNO-G) and the Pierre Auger Observatory search for EeV cosmogenic neutrinos, not yet detected. Measurements constrain the spectrum, flavor composition, neutrino–nucleon cross sections via Earth absorption, and physics beyond the Standard Model at otherwise inaccessible energies.
observables: diffuse flux normalisation and spectral index
ν–N cross section from Earth absorption
neutrino sky map and Galactic-plane emission
ultra-high-energy neutrino flux limits above 10^17 eV

name: Sterile neutrinos
question: Are there additional kinds of neutrino that do not feel the weak force, and could they explain puzzling results from short-distance neutrino experiments?
overview: Sterile neutrinos are hypothetical neutral fermions with no Standard Model gauge interactions that could mix with the three active neutrinos. Light (eV-scale) sterile neutrinos were motivated by anomalies: LSND's ν̄_e appearance (1990s), MiniBooNE's low-energy excess, the reactor antineutrino anomaly and the gallium anomaly (GALLEX and SAGE, reinforced by BEST in 2022). However, disappearance searches (MINOS+, IceCube, Daya Bay, PROSPECT, STEREO, DANSS) exclude most of the parameter space favoured by the appearance anomalies, MicroBooNE found no evidence that the MiniBooNE excess is due to electron neutrinos, and the reactor anomaly is largely explained by revised flux models. The Short-Baseline Neutrino programme (SBND, MicroBooNE, ICARUS) and JSNS² are testing the remaining regions. keV-scale sterile neutrinos are dark-matter candidates constrained by X-ray observations and beta-decay spectra.
observables: ν_e and ν̄_e appearance rates at short baselines
ν_μ and ν̄_e disappearance at short baselines

name: Direct neutrino mass measurement
question: How heavy is the neutrino? Can we measure its mass directly from the shape of a radioactive decay spectrum, without relying on cosmological models?
overview: Direct neutrino-mass experiments measure the kinematics of beta or electron-capture decay near the spectral endpoint, where the effective mass m_β = (Σ|U_ei|²m_i²)^1/2 distorts the spectrum; the method is model-independent, unlike the cosmological sum Σm_ν or the Majorana mass m_ββ from neutrinoless double beta decay. KATRIN, using gaseous molecular tritium and a MAC-E-filter spectrometer, set m_β < 0.45 eV (90% CL) in 2025 and targets a final sensitivity near 0.3 eV; the earlier Mainz and Troitsk experiments reached about 2 eV. Alternative approaches include cyclotron radiation emission spectroscopy (Project 8), 163Ho electron-capture calorimetry (ECHo, HOLMES) and the proposed relic-neutrino capture experiment PTOLEMY. Cosmology gives Σm_ν below roughly 0.1 eV under ΛCDM assumptions, while oscillation data require Σm_ν of at least about 0.06 eV.
observables: integral spectrum shape near the endpoint
spectrometer energy resolution and background rate

name: Neutrinoless double beta decay
question: Is the neutrino its own antiparticle? Seeing a nucleus decay by emitting two electrons and no neutrinos would prove it, and hint at how neutrinos acquire mass.
overview: Neutrinoless double beta decay (0νββ) would convert a nucleus (A,Z) into (A,Z+2) emitting two electrons and no neutrinos, violating lepton number by two units and demonstrating that neutrinos are Majorana particles. In the light-neutrino-exchange mechanism the rate scales with the square of the effective Majorana mass m_ββ and with nuclear matrix elements, whose theoretical uncertainty is a factor of two to three. No observation exists; leading half-life limits exceed 10^26 years from KamLAND-Zen (136Xe, above 3.8×10^26 yr), GERDA and MAJORANA DEMONSTRATOR (76Ge), CUORE (130Te) and EXO-200 (136Xe), with LEGEND-200 now running. Tonne-scale experiments (LEGEND-1000, nEXO, CUPID, KamLAND2-Zen, NEXT, SNO+) target sensitivities of 10^27–10^28 years, covering the inverted-ordering region m_ββ ≈ 15–50 meV. Backgrounds from 2νββ, radiogenic and cosmogenic sources require deep underground operation and ultra-pure materials.
observables: nuclear matrix elements and g_A quenching (theory inputs)

name: Coherent elastic neutrino–nucleus scattering
question: Can we see a neutrino bounce off an entire atomic nucleus at once, and what does that tell us about the nucleus and about possible new forces?
overview: Coherent elastic neutrino–nucleus scattering (CEvNS) is a neutral-current process in which a low-energy neutrino (tens of MeV or below) scatters off a nucleus as a whole, with a cross section that grows roughly as the square of the neutron number but yields only a keV-scale nuclear recoil. Predicted by Freedman in 1974, it was first observed by COHERENT in 2017 on CsI at the Oak Ridge Spallation Neutron Source (6.7σ), and later on argon and germanium. The process tests the Standard Model weak charge, constrains the neutron radius of nuclei, non-standard interactions, neutrino magnetic moments and light mediators, and sets the irreducible neutrino fog for direct dark-matter detection. Reactor CEvNS searches (CONUS, Dresden-II, TEXONO, νGeN, Ricochet) need sub-keV thresholds; in 2024 XENONnT and PandaX-4T each reported about 2.7σ indications of solar 8B CEvNS.
observables: N² scaling of the cross section
weak mixing angle at low momentum transfer
timing relative to the pulsed source

name: Direct dark matter detection
question: Can we catch a dark-matter particle from our own galaxy colliding with an atom in a detector deep underground?
overview: Direct detection experiments search for nuclear or electron recoils produced when Galactic dark matter passes through detectors operated deep underground to shield against cosmic rays. For WIMP masses of roughly 10 GeV to 10 TeV, dual-phase liquid-xenon time projection chambers (LZ, XENONnT, PandaX-4T) lead, with spin-independent cross-section limits near 2×10^-48 cm² at about 40 GeV (LZ, 2024), approaching the neutrino fog from solar and atmospheric neutrinos; liquid argon (DarkSide, DEAP-3600) and cryogenic crystals (SuperCDMS, CRESST, EDELWEISS) extend sensitivity to lower masses. Sub-GeV searches use electron recoils in skipper CCDs (SENSEI, DAMIC-M) or novel targets. The DAMA/LIBRA annual-modulation claim has not been confirmed by COSINE-100 and ANAIS-112 using the same NaI(Tl) target. Next-generation observatories (XLZD, DARWIN, ARGO) are being planned.
observables: spin-independent WIMP–nucleon cross section versus mass
spin-dependent WIMP–proton and WIMP–neutron cross sections
assumed local density (0.3 GeV/cm³) and velocity distribution

name: Indirect dark matter detection
question: If dark-matter particles annihilate or decay somewhere in space, can we spot the gamma rays, neutrinos or antimatter they would produce?
overview: Indirect detection searches for Standard Model particles produced by dark-matter annihilation or decay in astrophysical environments. Gamma-ray instruments (Fermi-LAT, H.E.S.S., MAGIC, VERITAS, HAWC, LHAASO) observe dwarf spheroidal galaxies, the Galactic Centre and galaxy clusters; combined Fermi-LAT dwarf-galaxy limits exclude thermal-relic annihilation cross sections for WIMP masses below about 100 GeV in some channels. Cosmic-ray antiprotons, positrons and antinuclei (AMS-02, PAMELA) and neutrinos from the Sun or the Galactic Centre (IceCube, Super-Kamiokande, ANTARES) give complementary constraints. The Galactic Centre GeV excess and the 3.5 keV X-ray line have been discussed as candidate signals but have plausible astrophysical or instrumental explanations. Interpretation depends strongly on the assumed dark-matter density profile (J-factor) and on astrophysical backgrounds.
observables: velocity-averaged annihilation cross section ⟨σv⟩ versus mass, per channel
neutrino flux from the Sun (spin-dependent capture)
Galactic Centre excess spectrum and morphology

name: Accelerator dark matter searches
question: Can particle accelerators make dark matter in the laboratory, and detect it either as missing energy or when it scatters in a detector downstream?
overview: Accelerators can produce dark matter or its mediators under controlled conditions, complementing direct and indirect searches. At the LHC, ATLAS and CMS look for missing transverse momentum recoiling against a jet, photon, Z or Higgs boson (mono-X signatures) and for mediator resonances, interpreted in simplified models. Electron-beam experiments (NA64, and the proposed LDMX) use missing-energy or missing-momentum signatures for sub-GeV dark matter coupled through a dark photon, while proton beam dumps and neutrino detectors (MiniBooNE-DM, COHERENT, SBND, the DUNE near detector) search for dark matter scattering downstream. BaBar and Belle II constrain invisible dark-photon decays via e+e−→γ+invisible. Results for light dark matter are compared with the thermal-relic target in the dimensionless coupling y = ε²α_D(m_χ/m_A′)^4.
observables: mediator mass versus coupling (g_q, g_χ) exclusions
y versus m_χ compared with thermal-relic targets
ε versus m_A′ for invisible dark photons
dark matter–electron and –nucleon scattering rates in downstream detectors

name: Axions and axion-like particles
question: Does an extremely light particle called the axion exist? It could solve a puzzle about the strong force and might also be the dark matter.
overview: The QCD axion is a pseudoscalar predicted by the Peccei–Quinn solution of the strong CP problem, with mass and couplings inversely proportional to the decay constant f_a; axion-like particles (ALPs) generalise this without the mass–coupling relation. Axions produced non-thermally in the early universe are a leading dark-matter candidate. Searches include haloscopes converting Galactic axions to microwave photons in a strong magnetic field (ADMX has excluded DFSZ-model couplings in parts of the 2.7–4.2 μeV range; HAYSTAC, CAPP, ORGAN, MADMAX and ALPHA cover other masses), helioscopes for solar axions (CAST; IAXO proposed), light-shining-through-walls (ALPS II), nuclear-spin and lumped-circuit techniques (CASPEr, ABRACADABRA, DMRadio), and astrophysical bounds from stellar cooling and SN 1987A. No detection has been made.
observables: axion–photon coupling g_aγγ versus mass m_a
haloscope power excess and scan rate

name: Dark photons and dark sectors
question: Is there a hidden sector of particles that barely interacts with ordinary matter, communicating only through a faint portal such as a dark photon?
overview: Dark sectors are hypothetical sets of particles neutral under the Standard Model gauge groups that couple to ordinary matter through portals: the vector portal (a dark photon A′ kinetically mixing with the photon with strength ε), the Higgs portal (dark scalars), the neutrino portal (heavy neutral leptons) and the axion portal. A visibly decaying dark photon appears as a narrow e+e− or μ+μ− resonance in electron fixed-target experiments (APEX, HPS, A1 at MAMI, NA64), meson decays (NA48/2, KLOE, BaBar, LHCb) and beam dumps (E137, E141, NA64, FASER, and the approved SHiP); invisible decays are covered under accelerator dark-matter searches. Exclusions cover much of the ε ~ 10^-3 region for masses below about 10 GeV, including the band once favoured by the muon g−2 anomaly. Related searches target dark Higgs bosons, millicharged particles and inelastic dark matter.
observables: kinetic-mixing parameter ε versus dark-photon mass m_A′
dark-scalar mixing angle sin²θ versus mass

name: Long-lived particles
question: Could new particles be hiding from collider searches because they travel metres before decaying, leaving signatures that detectors were not designed to catch?
overview: Long-lived particles (LLPs) are new states with macroscopic proper decay lengths, from millimetres to kilometres, arising in models with small couplings, compressed spectra or heavy mediators, such as hidden valleys, split supersymmetry, right-handed neutrinos and dark photons. Signatures include displaced vertices, disappearing or kinked tracks, delayed calorimeter deposits, trackless jets and stopped particles decaying out of time, requiring dedicated triggers and reconstruction that standard prompt searches lack. ATLAS, CMS and LHCb run broad LLP programmes, and forward or transverse detectors extend coverage to very weakly coupled light states: FASER and SND@LHC (which observed collider neutrinos in 2023), MoEDAL-MAPP, the proposed CODEX-b, ANUBIS and MATHUSLA, and the SHiP beam dump at the SPS, approved by CERN in 2024. Historical beam dumps such as CHARM, NuCal and E137 still set leading limits in some regions.
observables: lifetime cτ versus mass versus coupling exclusions
displaced-vertex invariant mass and track multiplicity

name: Heavy neutral leptons
question: Do heavy, mostly sterile partners of the neutrino exist? They could explain why neutrinos have mass and why the universe contains more matter than antimatter.
overview: Heavy neutral leptons (HNLs) are hypothetical neutral fermions that mix with active neutrinos with strength |U_α|², as in type-I seesaw models; masses from MeV to TeV are searched for, and GeV-scale HNLs could generate the baryon asymmetry through leptogenesis (νMSM). Signatures depend on mass: peak searches in pion and kaon decays (PIENU, NA62, KOTO), displaced decays in beam dumps and neutrino detectors (PS191, CHARM, NuTeV, T2K ND280, MicroBooNE, ArgoNeuT), prompt and displaced trilepton or dilepton-plus-jets final states at colliders (ATLAS, CMS, LHCb, Belle II, and DELPHI at LEP), and neutrinoless double beta decay for Majorana HNLs. Big Bang nucleosynthesis excludes very small mixings below about 0.1 GeV. SHiP, the DUNE near detector, FCC-ee and the HL-LHC would reach seesaw-motivated mixings at GeV-scale masses. No HNL has been observed.
observables: peak searches in K→μN and π→μN spectra

name: Charged lepton flavor violation
question: Can a muon turn into an electron without emitting neutrinos? That is essentially forbidden in the Standard Model, so seeing it would be unambiguous new physics.
overview: Charged lepton flavor violation (CLFV) processes such as μ→eγ, μ→eee, μ−N→e−N conversion, and τ→μγ or τ→3ℓ have Standard Model rates below 10^-50 induced by neutrino mixing, so any observation would signal new physics. MEG set B(μ+→e+γ) < 4.2×10^-13 (2016) and MEG II improved the combined limit to 1.5×10^-13 (2024); SINDRUM II limits muon-to-electron conversion in gold to below 7×10^-13. Mu3e at PSI aims at 10^-16 for μ→3e, and Mu2e (Fermilab) and COMET (J-PARC) target conversion sensitivities near 10^-17, four orders of magnitude beyond current limits. Belle II and LHCb pursue tau LFV at the 10^-9 level, and LFV is also sought in Z, Higgs, kaon and B-meson decays and in muonium–antimuonium conversion.
observables: muon-to-electron conversion rate R_μe on Al, Au, Ti

name: Muon precision physics (g−2, EDM)
question: Does the muon's magnetic moment match theory to better than a part in a million, and does the muon have an electric dipole moment? Either could expose new particles.
overview: The muon anomalous magnetic moment a_μ = (g−2)/2 is measured by storing polarised muons in a magnetic ring and observing the spin precession frequency relative to the cyclotron frequency. Fermilab's Muon g−2 experiment published its final result in 2025 with 127 ppb precision, consistent with BNL E821. The Standard Model prediction is limited by the hadronic vacuum polarisation: the 2020 data-driven (e+e−→hadrons) prediction differed from experiment by 4.2σ, but lattice-QCD calculations and the CMD-3 e+e− data shifted the 2025 Muon g−2 Theory Initiative prediction into agreement with experiment at about the 1σ level, so the hadronic input is now the central question. J-PARC plans an independent low-emittance measurement. Muon EDM searches (BNL limit 1.8×10^-19 e·cm; a frozen-spin experiment at PSI), the muon lifetime (MuLan) and Michel-parameter measurements complete the programme.
observables: muon lifetime τ_μ and Fermi constant G_F
Michel parameters ρ, δ, ξ, ξδ
hadronic vacuum polarisation a_μ^HVP (data-driven and lattice)

name: Cosmic rays
question: Where do the most energetic particles in the universe come from, and how are they accelerated to energies far beyond anything a laboratory can reach?
overview: Cosmic rays are charged nuclei (and electrons) arriving from space with energies from below 1 GeV to above 10^20 eV, following a steeply falling power-law spectrum with features: the knee near 3 PeV, the second knee, the ankle near 5 EeV, and a suppression above about 50 EeV consistent with the GZK effect and/or the exhaustion of sources. Direct measurements above the atmosphere (AMS-02, CALET, DAMPE, ISS-CREAM, balloon flights) resolve spectra and composition to about 100 TeV; extensive air-shower arrays (Pierre Auger Observatory, Telescope Array, IceTop, LHAASO, KASCADE-Grande, Tibet ASγ) cover higher energies through fluorescence, surface and radio detection. Auger observes a dipole anisotropy above 8 EeV pointing away from the Galactic Centre and a composition growing heavier above the ankle. Accelerator data (LHCf, NA61/SHINE) constrain the hadronic models used to interpret showers; the muon excess in showers remains unexplained.
observables: all-particle energy spectrum and its features
mass composition from X_max distributions and muon content
proton and helium spectra and spectral hardenings
muon number N_μ versus hadronic-model predictions

name: Gamma-ray astrophysics
question: What do the highest-energy photons from space tell us about black holes, exploding stars and the physics of extreme environments?
overview: Gamma-ray astronomy spans MeV to PeV photons. Fermi-LAT (20 MeV to above 300 GeV) has catalogued thousands of sources; imaging atmospheric Cherenkov telescopes (H.E.S.S., MAGIC, VERITAS, and the coming CTAO) cover roughly 30 GeV to 100 TeV with arcminute resolution; water-Cherenkov and hybrid arrays (HAWC, LHAASO, Tibet ASγ) survey the sky above about 1 TeV, and in 2021 LHAASO reported photons above 1 PeV from Galactic sources, including a 1.4 PeV photon from the Cygnus region. Sources include pulsar wind nebulae, supernova remnants, blazars, the Galactic diffuse emission and gamma-ray bursts, with GRB 221009A detected by LHAASO up to about 13 TeV. Particle-physics targets are dark-matter annihilation, axion–photon conversion in magnetic fields, Lorentz-invariance violation through energy-dependent arrival-time delays, and the extragalactic background light.
observables: source energy spectra dN/dE and cutoffs
light curves and variability time scales
dark-matter annihilation limits from dwarf galaxies

name: Multimessenger particle astrophysics
question: By combining light, neutrinos, cosmic rays and gravitational waves from the same cosmic event, what can we learn that no single messenger reveals?
overview: Multimessenger astrophysics combines electromagnetic, neutrino, cosmic-ray and gravitational-wave observations of the same sources. Landmarks include SN 1987A (neutrinos and light), GW170817 (the LIGO/Virgo binary neutron-star merger of 2017 with the gamma-ray burst GRB 170817A and a kilonova) and IceCube-170922A coincident with the flaring blazar TXS 0506+056 (2017, about 3σ). Neutrino follow-up of gravitational-wave events and gamma-ray follow-up of neutrino alerts, distributed through GCN and AMON, have so far produced no further confirmed neutrino–gravitational-wave coincidences. Physics goals include identifying the sources of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays through neutrinos, constraining the speed of gravity and neutrino properties through arrival-time differences, and testing Lorentz invariance. The SNEWS 2.0 network prepares a coordinated alert for the next Galactic supernova.
observables: neutrino upper limits on isotropic-equivalent energy for GW events

name: Heavy-ion physics and the quark–gluon plasma
question: What was the universe made of a few microseconds after the Big Bang, and how does a hot soup of free quarks and gluons behave?
overview: Colliding heavy nuclei at RHIC (Au+Au up to √s_NN = 200 GeV) and the LHC (Pb+Pb at 2.76 and 5.02 TeV, 5.36 TeV in Run 3) produces the quark–gluon plasma (QGP), a deconfined state of QCD matter above a transition temperature of about 155 MeV. It behaves as a near-perfect fluid with a shear-viscosity-to-entropy ratio close to the conjectured quantum bound, evidenced by large elliptic and higher-order anisotropic flow, and it quenches jets: high-p_T hadron and jet yields are suppressed (R_AA) relative to scaled proton–proton collisions. Heavy quarks and quarkonia probe thermalisation and colour screening, including J/ψ regeneration at the LHC. Current frontiers are collectivity in small systems (p+Pb, high-multiplicity p+p), the search for a QCD critical point in the RHIC Beam Energy Scan, vorticity effects such as Λ polarisation, and the sPHENIX and upgraded ALICE programmes.

name: Detector R&D and technology milestones
question: Which new detector technologies make future discoveries possible, and which milestones show that a technique is ready for a full-scale experiment?
overview: Detector R&D develops the sensors, readout and infrastructure that set what experiments can measure. Recent milestones include kilotonne-scale liquid-argon time projection chambers (ICARUS T600; ProtoDUNE single- and dual-phase prototypes at the CERN Neutrino Platform, 2018–2020), silicon sensors with about 30 ps timing (LGADs for the ATLAS HGTD and CMS MTD), monolithic CMOS pixel sensors (ALICE ITS2 and the bent-wafer ITS3), large silicon-photomultiplier arrays, gadolinium-loaded and water-based scintillators, and high-pressure gaseous TPCs. Priorities in the 2021 ECFA Detector R&D Roadmap and the Snowmass 2021 Instrumentation Frontier report include picosecond timing, radiation-hard sensors for the HL-LHC and future colliders, noble-liquid scaling to tens of kilotonnes, quantum sensors for light dark matter and axions, radiopure low-background materials, high-throughput trigger and data-acquisition systems using machine learning, and dual-readout or highly granular calorimetry.
observables: photon detection efficiency and dark-count rate
electron drift lifetime and purity in noble liquids
power per channel and material budget (X/X_0)
detector mass or active volume achieved
